evidence.thesis: The paper introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction architecture built entirely on attention mechanisms with no recurrence or convolutions. It matches or beats the best prior models on machine translation while being more parallelizable and far cheaper to train.
evidence.plain_summary: Earlier translation systems relied on recurrent or convolutional neural networks, which process text step by step and are slow to train. The authors propose the Transformer, which uses only attention (including multi-head self-attention) to relate every word in a sentence to every other word, plus positional encodings to retain word order. On WMT 2014 English-to-German it reaches 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 BLEU above the previous best results including ensembles. On English-to-French it reaches 41.8 BLEU for a single model, with a fraction of the training cost of earlier systems. Ablation experiments show which design choices matter, and the model also performs well on English constituency parsing, suggesting it generalizes beyond translation.
evidence.research_question: Can a sequence transduction model that relies solely on attention, without recurrent or convolutional layers, achieve better quality and be much more parallelizable and efficient to train than existing recurrent and convolutional models?

claims.statement: The Transformer outperforms the BerkeleyParser even when trained only on the 40K-sentence WSJ training set, unlike RNN seq2seq models.
Only a small number of experiments were performed to select dropout, learning rates and beam size for parsing, with other parameters unchanged from the English-to-German base model.
Regularization includes residual dropout (Pdrop=0.1 for base) and label smoothing of 0.1, which hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU.
Base models used checkpoint averaging of the last 5 checkpoints, big models of the last 20, with beam search of size 4 and length penalty 0.6.
Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads.
A 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performs surprisingly well on constituency parsing, better than all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar.
Table 2 shows the Transformer achieves better BLEU than previous state-of-the-art models at a fraction of the training cost.

Constituency parsing is challenging because outputs have strong structural constraints and are significantly longer than input, and RNN seq2seq models had not attained state-of-the-art in small-data regimes.
The authors plan to extend the Transformer to other modalities, investigate local restricted attention for large inputs, and make generation less sequential.
Reducing the attention key size dk hurts model quality, which the authors interpret as suggesting a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may be beneficial.
Bigger models are better and dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting.
Training used Adam with a learning rate schedule that increases linearly for 4000 warmup steps then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of step number.
The Transformer is more parallelizable and requires significantly less time to train than recurrent or convolutional models.
Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, which a single head's averaging inhibits.
Restricting self-attention to a neighborhood of size r would increase maximum path length to O(n/r); the authors leave this for future work.
Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention, though theoretical complexity is similar.

Multi-head attention linearly projects queries, keys and values h times, applies attention in parallel, and concatenates and projects the outputs; h=8 with dk=dv=64 is used, keeping computational cost similar to single-head attention.
The decoder adds a third sub-layer attending over the encoder output and masks self-attention to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions, preserving auto-regressive predictions.

Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimensionality d, and connect all positions with a constant number of sequential operations.
Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results to sinusoidal encodings.
The model injects position information using sinusoidal positional encodings added to input embeddings.
Models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5M sentence pairs, ~37000 BPE vocabulary) and English-French (36M sentences, 32000 word-piece vocabulary).
The Transformer generalizes to English constituency parsing with both large and limited training data.

The encoder and decoder each consist of a stack of N=6 identical layers; encoder layers have a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward sub-layer with residual connections and layer normalization, with dmodel=512.

In ConvS2S and ByteNet, the number of operations to relate distant positions grows linearly and logarithmically respectively, making long-distance dependencies harder to learn; the Transformer reduces this to a constant number of operations.
Self-attention could yield more interpretable models; individual attention heads clearly learn different tasks and many appear related to syntactic and semantic structure.
The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three ways: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention, and masked decoder self-attention.
Base models were trained for 100,000 steps (12 hours) and big models for 300,000 steps (3.5 days) on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs.
The Transformer achieves 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, improving over the existing best results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU.

The Transformer establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU of 41.8 on WMT 2014 English-to-French after 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training cost of the best literature models.
The model shares the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation.
Scaled dot-product attention computes dot products of queries with keys, divides by sqrt(dk), and applies softmax to obtain weights on the values.
The authors hypothesized sinusoidal encodings would let the model easily learn to attend by relative positions, and chose them because they may allow extrapolation to longer sequences.
Even the Transformer base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles on English-to-German at a fraction of the training cost.

The text in Section 6.1 reports a BLEU of 41.0 for the big model on English-to-French, outperforming all previously published single models at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous state-of-the-art.
The authors suspect that for large dk dot products grow large, pushing softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, motivating scaling by 1/sqrt(dk).
The sequential nature of recurrent models precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths.
The Transformer is a new network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
The authors claim, to the best of their knowledge, that the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention without sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution.

glossary_terms.definition: An attention mechanism in which a sequence attends to itself: each position is related to every other position in the same sequence to build a representation of that sequence. Also called intra-attention.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence.

glossary_terms.definition: The attention function used in the Transformer. It takes dot products of a query with all keys, divides them by the square root of the key dimension, and applies a softmax to get weights for combining the values.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

glossary_terms.definition: A mechanism that runs several attention functions in parallel on different learned linear projections of the queries, keys and values. The outputs are concatenated and projected again, letting the model attend to different kinds of information at once.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

glossary_terms.definition: The neural network architecture proposed in the paper, which relies entirely on attention mechanisms and dispenses with recurrence and convolutions.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

glossary_terms.definition: A property of a model that generates output one element at a time, using the previously generated elements as additional input when producing the next one.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): The task of converting one sequence into another sequence, such as translating a sentence from one language to another.
A model structure in which an encoder maps an input sequence to continuous representations and a decoder uses them to generate an output sequence one element at a time.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations (x1, ..., xn) to a sequence of continuous representations z = (z1, ..., zn).

glossary_terms.definition: A function that maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output vector, computed as a weighted sum of the values with weights determined by how well the query matches each key.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

glossary_terms.definition: An attention function that computes the compatibility between a query and a key using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): A shortcut that adds the input of a layer to its output, helping gradients flow and making deep networks easier to train.
General term (not defined in this paper): A technique that normalizes the activations across the features of a layer for each example, stabilizing and speeding up training.
General term (not defined in this paper): A function that converts a vector of real numbers into a probability distribution, with positive values that sum to one.
In the decoder's self-attention, the setting of softmax inputs corresponding to illegal (future-position) connections to −∞, so that predictions for a position depend only on earlier positions.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections.

glossary_terms.definition: A fully connected network applied identically and separately to each position, consisting of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: This consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): Rectified Linear Unit, an activation function that outputs max(0, x), i.e., zero for negative inputs and the input itself otherwise.
General term (not defined in this paper): Learned vector representations of discrete tokens (such as words or subwords) that let a neural network process them numerically.

Information about the position of tokens that is added to the input embeddings, since the model has no recurrence or convolution to capture order. The paper uses sine and cosine functions of different frequencies.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): A neural network that processes a sequence step by step, maintaining a hidden state that is updated from the previous state and the current input.
General term (not defined in this paper): A neural network that applies learned filters (kernels) over local neighborhoods of the input, sharing weights across positions.
The longest length of the path that forward and backward signals must traverse between any two input and output positions in a network; shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): Convolutions whose kernels skip input positions at regular intervals, enlarging the receptive field without adding parameters.
General term (not defined in this paper): Convolutions factored into a depthwise (per-channel) step followed by a pointwise step, greatly reducing computational cost.
General term (not defined in this paper): A subword tokenization method that iteratively merges the most frequent pairs of symbols to build a vocabulary of subword units.
General term (not defined in this paper): A subword vocabulary approach that splits words into smaller frequently occurring units, so rare words can be represented by pieces.
General term (not defined in this paper): A metric for evaluating machine translation quality by measuring n-gram overlap between a system's output and reference translations; higher is better.
General term (not defined in this paper): A stochastic gradient-based optimization algorithm that adapts learning rates per parameter using estimates of first and second moments of the gradients.
The number of initial training steps during which the learning rate is increased linearly, after which it decreases proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: This corresponds to increasing the learning rate linearly for the first warmup_steps training steps, and decreasing it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number.

glossary_terms.definition: Dropout applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized, and also to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: We apply dropout [33] to the output of each sub-layer, before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalized.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): A regularization technique that randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training to reduce overfitting.
A regularization technique that softens the target labels during training. The paper notes it hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): A measure of how well a probability model predicts a sample; lower values indicate better predictions.
General term (not defined in this paper): A decoding algorithm that keeps the several most probable partial output sequences (the beam) at each step instead of only the single best.
General term (not defined in this paper): An adjustment applied during beam search that modifies sequence scores based on output length, to avoid favoring too-short or too-long outputs.
Producing a single model by averaging the parameters of the last several saved checkpoints during training.
glossary_terms.source_excerpt: For the base models, we used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints, which were written at 10-minute intervals.

glossary_terms.definition: General term (not defined in this paper): A combination of multiple separately trained models whose predictions are merged to improve performance.
General term (not defined in this paper): Floating point operations, a count of arithmetic operations used as a measure of computational cost.
General term (not defined in this paper): The task of analyzing a sentence to produce a tree that groups words into nested phrases (constituents) according to its syntactic structure.
General term (not defined in this paper): A training setting that uses both labeled data and a larger amount of unlabeled or automatically labeled data.
General term (not defined in this paper): An evaluation score that is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
General term (not defined in this paper): The task of determining which earlier word or phrase a pronoun or similar expression (like 'its') refers to.
General term (not defined in this paper): When a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, and performs worse on unseen data.

generated_sections.title: Self-attention versus recurrent layers
generated_sections.content: The paper compares layer types by sequential operations and speed. A self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations. The paper also states that self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d, which it says is most often the case with sentence representations.

generated_sections.title: Overview and Motivation
generated_sections.content: The paper proposes the Transformer, a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely. The motivation comes from the limits of recurrent models: their inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths because memory constraints limit batching across examples. Convolutional alternatives such as ConvS2S and ByteNet need a number of operations to relate distant positions that grows linearly and logarithmically with distance respectively, making long-range dependencies harder to learn. The Transformer reduces this to a constant number of operations, at the cost of reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions. The authors state that, to the best of their knowledge, it is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention without sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution.

generated_sections.title: Architecture: Encoder, Decoder and Attention
generated_sections.content: Both the encoder and decoder are stacks of N=6 identical layers with dmodel=512. Encoder layers combine a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward sub-layer, each wrapped with residual connections and layer normalization. The decoder adds a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder output and masks its self-attention so positions cannot attend to subsequent positions, preserving auto-regressive prediction. Multi-head attention is used in three ways: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention, and masked decoder self-attention. The model also shares one weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation.

generated_sections.title: Scaled Dot-Product and Multi-Head Attention
generated_sections.content: The core operation is scaled dot-product attention: dot products of the query with all keys are divided by sqrt(dk), and a softmax gives the weights on the values. Dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice than additive attention despite similar theoretical complexity. The authors suspect that for large dk the dot products grow large and push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, which motivates the scaling. Multi-head attention linearly projects queries, keys and values h times, applies attention in parallel, then concatenates and projects the outputs. With h=8 and dk=dv=64, computational cost remains similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality. The authors interpret multi-head attention as letting the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, which averaging in a single head inhibits.

generated_sections.title: Positional Encoding and Why Self-Attention
generated_sections.content: Because the model has no recurrence or convolution, position information is injected via sinusoidal positional encodings added to input embeddings. The authors hypothesized this would let the model easily learn to attend by relative positions and chose it because it may allow extrapolation to longer sequences. Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results. On the efficiency side, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations whereas a recurrent layer needs O(n), and self-attention is faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimensionality d. The authors also suggest self-attention could yield more interpretable models, noting that individual heads clearly learn different tasks and many seem related to syntactic and semantic structure.

generated_sections.title: Training Setup
generated_sections.content: Models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5M sentence pairs, ~37000 BPE vocabulary) and English-French (36M sentences, 32000 word-piece vocabulary). Training ran on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs: base models for 100,000 steps (12 hours) and big models for 300,000 steps (3.5 days). Optimization used Adam with a learning rate that increases linearly for 4000 warmup steps and then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. Regularization includes residual dropout (0.1 for the base model) and label smoothing of 0.1, which hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU. At inference, base models average the last 5 checkpoints and big models the last 20, using beam search of size 4 and length penalty 0.6.

generated_sections.title: Machine Translation Results
generated_sections.content: On WMT 2014 English-to-German the Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. Even the base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles at a fraction of the training cost. On English-to-French, the paper reports a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU of 41.8 after 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training cost of the best literature models. The text of Section 6.1 separately reports 41.0 BLEU for the big model, outperforming all previously published single models at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous state-of-the-art. Overall, the Transformer achieves better BLEU than previous state-of-the-art models at a fraction of the training cost, and it is more parallelizable and significantly faster to train than recurrent or convolutional models.

generated_sections.title: Ablation Findings
generated_sections.content: Ablation experiments identify which design choices matter. Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads. Reducing the attention key size dk hurts quality, which the authors read as suggesting that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility function than dot product may help. Bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting. Swapping sinusoidal encodings for learned positional embeddings made almost no difference.

generated_sections.title: Generalization to Constituency Parsing
generated_sections.content: To test generalization, the authors apply the Transformer to English constituency parsing, a task that is challenging because outputs have strong structural constraints and are significantly longer than the input, and because RNN seq2seq models had not reached state-of-the-art in small-data regimes. Only a small number of experiments were run to select dropout, learning rates and beam size, with other parameters unchanged from the English-to-German base model. Despite little task-specific tuning, a 4-layer Transformer performs surprisingly well, better than all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar. Unlike RNN seq2seq models, it outperforms the BerkeleyParser even when trained only on the 40K-sentence WSJ set, supporting the claim that it generalizes with both large and limited training data.

generated_sections.title: Limitations and Future Directions
generated_sections.content: The authors acknowledge directions left open. They plan to extend the Transformer to input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video, and to make generation less sequential. Restricting self-attention to a neighborhood of size r would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r), an approach they leave for future work. The trade-off of reduced effective resolution from averaging attention-weighted positions is also noted.

generated_sections.title: Reading one word at a time is slow
generated_sections.content: Earlier translation systems relied on recurrent or convolutional neural networks. Recurrent models work through a sentence step by step, and this sequential nature prevents parallelization within a training example. The problem gets worse for longer sentences, because memory limits how many examples can be batched together. The authors asked a bold question: can a model built only on attention, with no recurrence and no convolutions, do the job better and train far faster?

generated_sections.title: An encoder, a decoder and attention everywhere
generated_sections.content: The Transformer has an encoder and a decoder, each a stack of six identical layers. Each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention step and a position-wise feed-forward step, wrapped in residual connections and layer normalization. The decoder adds a third step that looks at the encoder's output. It also masks its own self-attention so a position cannot peek at later positions, which keeps predictions auto-regressive. Because attention has no built-in sense of order, the model adds sine and cosine position signals to the word embeddings. Multi-head attention is used in three ways: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention and masked decoder self-attention.

generated_sections.title: Every word looks at every other word
generated_sections.content: Attention scores how relevant each word is to each other word. The model compares a query with all keys using dot products, divides each by the square root of the key size dk, and applies a softmax to get weights on the values. The authors suspect that for large dk the dot products grow large and push the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients, which is why the scaling is there. Multi-head attention runs this several times in parallel with different learned projections. The paper uses 8 heads with 64 dimensions each, so the cost stays similar to a single head. Several heads let the model attend to different kinds of information at once, which a single head's averaging inhibits.

generated_sections.title: Limits and what comes next

They also plan to extend the Transformer to other modalities such as images, audio and video, and to make generation less sequential.

generated_sections.title: The problem: sequential computation in recurrent models
generated_sections.content: General background (not a claim of this paper): sequence transduction tasks such as machine translation map an input sequence to an output sequence. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have traditionally been used for this, processing a sequence one position at a time. The paper reports that this inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples. This becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, because memory constraints limit batching across examples. This limitation motivates the paper's proposal, the Transformer, a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

generated_sections.title: Relating distant positions: convolutional models and path length
generated_sections.content: General background: a central question for sequence models is how easily they learn dependencies between positions that are far apart. The paper notes that in convolutional models such as ConvS2S and ByteNet, the number of operations needed to relate signals from two arbitrary positions grows with their distance, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes long-distance dependencies harder to learn. The Transformer reduces this to a constant number of operations. The paper acknowledges a cost: reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions.

generated_sections.title: Scaled dot-product attention and why dot-product is used
generated_sections.content: General background: attention lets a model compute, for each position, a weighted combination of values, where the weights depend on how well a query matches a set of keys. In the paper's scaled dot-product attention, the query's dot products with all keys are computed, each is divided by √dk, and a softmax produces the weights on the values. The paper contrasts dot-product attention with additive attention: the two are similar in theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice.

generated_sections.title: Multi-head attention
generated_sections.content: Rather than a single attention function, multi-head attention linearly projects the queries, keys and values h times, applies attention in parallel to each projection, then concatenates and projects the outputs. The paper uses h = 8 heads with dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64. Because each head has reduced dimension, the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality.

generated_sections.title: Encoder-decoder structure and the three uses of attention
generated_sections.content: General background: many sequence transduction models use an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that generates the output. In this paper, both the encoder and decoder are stacks of N = 6 identical layers with dmodel = 512. Encoder layers have a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward sub-layer. Each sub-layer is wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization, so its output is LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The decoder adds a third sub-layer that attends over the encoder output, and its self-attention is masked so positions cannot attend to subsequent positions, preserving auto-regressive prediction. Overall, the Transformer uses multi-head attention in three ways: encoder-decoder attention, encoder self-attention, and masked decoder self-attention.

generated_sections.title: Positional encodings and shared embeddings
generated_sections.content: General background: because attention alone does not encode word order, position information must be injected. The paper does this with sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, added to the input embeddings. The model also shares the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, similar to prior work.

generated_sections.title: Training data and hardware setup
generated_sections.content: The models were trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset (about 4.5 million sentence pairs, with a roughly 37000-token BPE vocabulary) and the much larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset (36M sentences, with a 32000 word-piece vocabulary). Training ran on one machine with 8 P100 GPUs. Base models trained for 100,000 steps (12 hours) and big models for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).

generated_sections.title: Optimization and regularization
generated_sections.content: General background: Adam is a widely used gradient-based optimizer, and dropout and label smoothing are common regularization techniques. The paper uses Adam with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10⁻⁹. Its learning rate increases linearly for 4000 warmup steps, then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. For regularization it uses residual dropout (Pdrop = 0.1 for the base model) and label smoothing of 0.1. The paper notes that label smoothing hurts perplexity, since the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

generated_sections.title: Inference: checkpoint averaging and beam search
generated_sections.content: General background: beam search keeps several candidate output sequences while decoding, and a length penalty adjusts how outputs of different lengths are scored. The paper uses a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints for base models (written at 10-minute intervals) and the last 20 for big models. It decodes with beam search of size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6.

generated_sections.title: Constituency parsing as a test of generalization
generated_sections.content: General background: constituency parsing assigns a hierarchical phrase structure to a sentence. The paper describes the task as challenging because the output is subject to strong structural constraints and is significantly longer than the input. It also notes that RNN sequence-to-sequence models have not attained state-of-the-art results in small-data regimes. For parsing, only a small number of experiments were performed to select dropout, learning rates and beam size on the Section 22 development set, with other parameters unchanged from the English-to-German base model.

generated_sections.title: When to reach for this approach
generated_sections.content: The Transformer is a network architecture based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Consider it when you are working on sequence transduction problems such as machine translation, where the paper reports better quality than previous state-of-the-art models along with greater parallelizability and substantially shorter training time than recurrent or convolutional architectures. The paper also reports that it generalizes to English constituency parsing, so it is not limited to translation.

generated_sections.title: What you need: data and compute
generated_sections.content: The paper trained on standard WMT 2014 datasets: English-German with about 4.5 million sentence pairs (about 37000-token BPE vocabulary) and the much larger English-French set of 36M sentences (32000 word-piece vocabulary). Hardware was one machine with 8 P100 GPUs. Base models trained for 100,000 steps (12 hours) and big models for 300,000 steps (3.5 days). If your setup is comparable, these figures give a realistic sense of the budget required.

generated_sections.title: Starting configuration
generated_sections.content: The base configuration uses an encoder and decoder each with a stack of N=6 identical layers and dmodel=512. Multi-head attention uses h=8 heads with dk=dv=64, which keeps computational cost similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality. The decoder adds attention over the encoder output and masks self-attention so that predictions remain auto-regressive. Position information is injected with sinusoidal encodings; learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results, so either choice is reasonable. The model also shares one weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation.

generated_sections.title: Training recipe to follow
generated_sections.content: The paper trained with the Adam optimizer, with a learning rate that increases linearly over 4000 warmup steps and then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. Regularization consisted of residual dropout (0.1 for the base model) and label smoothing of 0.1; label smoothing hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU, so do not judge it by perplexity alone. Dropout was found very helpful against over-fitting, and bigger models performed better.

generated_sections.title: Inference settings
generated_sections.content: For decoding, the paper used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints for base models (written at 10-minute intervals) or the last 20 for big models, with beam search of size 4 and length penalty 0.6.

generated_sections.title: Design choices that matter
generated_sections.content: Attention head count is worth checking: single-head attention was 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, but quality also dropped with too many heads. So avoid both extremes rather than assuming more heads is better.

generated_sections.title: Results to expect on translation
generated_sections.content: The big Transformer reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, improving over the best previous results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. Even the base model surpassed all previously published models and ensembles there at a fraction of the training cost. On English-to-French, the paper reports a new single-model state of the art of 41.8 BLEU after 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training cost of the best literature models. Note that the text of Section 6.1 states 41.0 BLEU for the big model, at less than 1/4 the training cost of the previous state of the art, so the two figures differ within the paper itself.

generated_sections.title: Applying it to other tasks such as parsing
generated_sections.content: For English constituency parsing, a 4-layer Transformer with little task-specific tuning performed surprisingly well, better than all previously reported models except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar. Only a small number of experiments were used to select dropout, learning rates and beam size, with other parameters unchanged from the English-to-German base model. Unlike RNN sequence-to-sequence models, it outperformed the BerkeleyParser even when trained only on the roughly 40K-sentence WSJ training set, which makes it a candidate when labeled data is limited.

stories.title: Attention Is All You Need: The Machine Translation Shortcut
stories.dek: A translation model drops step-by-step processing and lets every word look at every other word, and it gets better and faster to train.

closing.body: The Transformer showed that attention alone can beat recurrent and convolutional translation systems on quality while training much faster. It also carried over to English constituency parsing. Open questions remain. The authors want to extend it beyond text to images, audio and video, to try local restricted attention for very large inputs, and to make generation less sequential.
closing.title: What to take away

steps.formula: MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) W^O, where head_i = Attention(Q W_i^Q, K W_i^K, V W_i^V)
steps.explanation: Multi-head attention linearly projects queries, keys and values h times, applies attention in parallel on each projection, then concatenates the head outputs and projects them again.
The paper uses h = 8 parallel heads, and each head's key/value dimension is the model dimension divided by h. With dmodel = 512 this gives 64.

steps.formula: cost(h heads, d_k = d_model/h) ≈ cost(1 head, full d_model); single-head ≈ best − 0.9 BLEU
steps.explanation: Because each head has a reduced dimension, the total computational cost is similar to single-head attention at full dimensionality. The ablation reports that single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads.
Training uses the Adam optimizer with the stated hyperparameters.

The learning rate increases linearly for the first 4000 warmup steps and then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. This is a verbal description of the schedule's shape, not a quoted formula.

Base models were trained for 100,000 steps (12 hours) and big models for 300,000 steps (3.5 days). The metrics give step times of 0.4 s for base and 1.0 s for big, which are consistent with these totals.
The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network.
Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.

Regularization uses residual dropout with Pdrop = 0.1 for the base model, and label smoothing of 0.1. Label smoothing hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but it improves accuracy and BLEU.
The big Transformer reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German. The best previous ensemble in Table 2 (ConvS2S Ensemble) scores 26.36 BLEU.

The base model scores 27.3 BLEU on English-to-German. This is also above the best previous ensemble's 26.36, consistent with the claim that even the base model surpasses all previously published models and ensembles.

steps.formula: EN-FR big: 41.8 BLEU, 3.5 days on 8 GPUs
steps.explanation: On English-to-French the big model sets a new single-model state of the art of 41.8 BLEU after 3.5 days on eight GPUs, at a small fraction of the training cost of the best literature models.

Training cost from Table 2 for English-to-German: 3.3·10^18 FLOPs for the base model and 2.3·10^19 FLOPs for the big model. The Transformer outperforms previous state-of-the-art models in BLEU at a fraction of their training cost.

learning_interactives.title: Training time from step count and step time
learning_interactives.description: Estimates wall-clock training time as steps times seconds per step. The paper reports base models at 100,000 steps with 0.4 s per step (about 12 hours) and big models at 300,000 steps with 1.0 s per step (about 3.5 days) on 8 P100 GPUs. The slider ranges and step sizes are illustrative, not values reported in the paper. The default settings correspond to the base model.

learning_interactives.title: Multi-head attention: per-head dimension and cost
learning_interactives.description: Shows how the per-head key/value dimension dk = dv = dmodel/h changes with the number of heads h, and how the total projection width h*dk stays equal to dmodel, so cost stays similar to single-head attention with full dimensionality. The paper's base values are dmodel = 512 and h = 8 (giving dk = 64). The slider ranges and step sizes are illustrative choices, not values reported in the paper; the paper only reports the h = 8 setting and that single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting while too many heads also hurts.

learning_interactives.title: Scaled dot-product attention scaling factor
learning_interactives.description: Explores the 1/sqrt(dk) divisor applied to query-key dot products before the softmax. You choose dk and a raw dot-product value and see the scaled score. The paper's default dk is 64. The slider ranges, the raw dot product range and the steps are illustrative, not values reported in the paper.

learning_interactives.title: Learning rate schedule with warmup
learning_interactives.description: Explores the paper's schedule: the learning rate rises linearly for warmup_steps and then decays proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number, i.e. lrate = dmodel^-0.5 * min(step^-0.5, step*warmup^-1.5). The paper uses warmup_steps = 4000 and dmodel = 512. The slider ranges and step sizes are illustrative, not values reported in the paper. Training steps of 100,000 (base) and 300,000 (big) are reported, but the full range of the step slider is illustrative.

learning_interactives.title: BLEU margin over previous best on English-to-German
learning_interactives.description: Computes the Transformer's BLEU margin over a comparison system on WMT 2014 English-to-German. The paper reports 28.4 BLEU for Transformer (big), 27.3 for the base model, 26.36 for the ConvS2S ensemble and 23.75 for ByteNet in Table 2. The slider ranges and steps are illustrative; only the default values come from the paper. Defaults compare the big model against the ConvS2S ensemble, a margin of over 2 BLEU as claimed in the paper.

source_references.excerpt: We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.

Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-
to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including
ensembles, by over 2 BLEU.

outperforms the best previously reported models (including ensembles) by more than 2.0
BLEU, establishing a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.4.

our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after
training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the
best models from the literature.

our big model achieves a BLEU score of 41.0,
outperforming all of the previously published single models, at less than 1/4 the training cost of the
previous state-of-the-art model.

Even our base model
surpasses all previously published models and ensembles, at a fraction of the training cost of any of
the competitive models.

Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to
be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly
less time to train.

For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based
on recurrent or convolutional layers.

We show that the Transformer generalizes well to
other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with
large and limited training data.

This inherently
sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer
sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

In these models,
the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows
in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet.

In the Transformer this is
reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due
to averaging attention-weighted positions

To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying
entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-
aligned RNNs or convolution.

The encoder is composed of a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each layer has two
sub-layers.

That is, the output of each sub-layer is
LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))

We also modify the self-attention
sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions.

We compute the dot products of the
query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the
values.

While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is
much faster and more space-efficient in practice

We suspect that for large values of
dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has
extremely small gradients 4.

In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use
dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

Due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost
is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation
subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.
The Transformer uses multi-head attention in three different ways:

we share the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax
linear transformation, similar to [30].
In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies:

We
chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by
relative positions

We chose the sinusoidal version
because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered
during training.

versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))

and observe nearly identical
results to the base model.

As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially
executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

sentence representations

This would increase the maximum
path length to O(n/r). We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic
and semantic structure of the sentences.

We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million
sentence pairs.

For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT
2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece
vocabulary [38].
We trained the base models for a total of 100,000 steps or 12 hours.

The big models were trained for 300,000 steps
(3.5 days).
We used the Adam optimizer [20] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10−9.

We used
warmup_steps = 4000.

For the base model, we use a rate of
Pdrop = 0.1.

This
hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the
English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.

For the base models, we used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints, which
were written at 10-minute intervals. For the big models, we averaged the last 20 checkpoints.

We
used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 [38].

While single-head
attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.

we observe that reducing the attention key size dk hurts model quality. This
suggests that determining compatibility is not easy and that a more sophisticated compatibility
function than dot product may be beneficial.
bigger models are better, and dropout is very helpful in avoiding over-fitting.

Our results in Table 4 show that despite the lack of task-specific tuning our model performs sur-
prisingly well, yielding better results than all previously reported models with the exception of the
Recurrent Neural Network Grammar [8].

In contrast to RNN sequence-to-sequence models [37], the Transformer outperforms the Berkeley-
Parser [29] even when training only on the WSJ training set of 40K sentences.

This task presents specific challenges: the output is subject to strong structural
constraints and is significantly longer than the input.

Furthermore, RNN sequence-to-sequence
models have not been able to attain state-of-the-art results in small-data regimes [37].

We performed only a small number of experiments to select the dropout, both attention and residual
(section 5.4), learning rates and beam size on the Section 22 development set

We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and
to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs
such as images, audio and video.
Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours.
